properties.headline: Radar maps a burn scar of about 31 km² in Big Sur
properties.subtitle: Plaskett Fire · Los Padres National Forest
properties.confidence_note: Exploratory thresholds on the drop in L-band cross-polarised radar, not a validated burn map
properties.summary: Comparing NISAR's radar pass on 3 October 2026 with 16 August 2026, before the fire, about 31 km² lost so much cross-polarised signal that it is likely burned, and another 15 km² is possibly burned. Healthy vegetation returns a strong cross-polarised (HV) radar signal from the leaves and branches of forest and chaparral; when fire removes them, the signal drops by several decibels.
causes: Fire burning through forest and chaparral canopy, removing leaves and branches
Severe burns on steep slopes leaving bare soil and standing dead trunks
Smaller drops can also come from drying vegetation or a change in soil moisture
properties.why_it_matters: Burned slopes above Highway 1 are prone to debris flows and landslides once the winter rains arrive. Knowing where the canopy is gone helps decide which roads, creeks and communities need protection first.
properties.next_step: Compare with the official fire perimeter, Sentinel-2 burn-severity (dNBR) maps and NASA FIRMS hotspots before treating the outline as the burn scar.
properties.explanation:
NISAR passed over Big Sur 6 times between 16 August 2026 and 15 October 2026, all from the same track and look direction so the passes can be compared. Each pass was compared with 16 August 2026, the last pass before the fire started. Healthy vegetation returns a strong cross-polarised (HV) radar signal from the leaves and branches of forest and chaparral; when fire removes them, the signal drops by several decibels. Before comparing, the radar brightness was averaged over about 100 m to reduce speckle. Pixels whose HV fell by more than 3 dB are counted as likely burned, and by 2–3 dB as possibly burned.

While the fire was burning, the likely-burned area read 0.3 km² on 28 August 2026, 19 km² on 9 September 2026 and 25 km² on 21 September 2026. On 3 October 2026, the first pass after the fire period, it was 31 km², with 15 km² more possibly burned. The last pass, on 15 October 2026, read 41 km², so the area kept growing after the fire period. That can mean the fire was still spreading at its edges, or that scorched vegetation kept drying out and losing its leaves. On the map, the burned patches are filled in two colours, likely and possibly burned; together they cover about 46 km². The story outline is drawn around them.

Fire reports put the fire at about 121 km² (29,862 acres on 8 September 2026, 47% contained). The radar's likely-burned area is 26% of that, and 38% with the possibly burned pixels added. A reported fire area is the whole perimeter: it includes unburned islands and ground fire under a canopy that survived, where the radar signal barely changes, so the radar is expected to flag less than the reported area. Source: https://bigsurkate.blog/2026/09/08/.

What this does not say: these are threshold rules on radar brightness, not a verified burn-severity map. Drying vegetation, a change in soil moisture after rain and wind in the vegetation can also lower the signal. Steep slopes facing away from the satellite are poorly seen, and the fire may have burned there too. Treat the outline as where to look first, not as the official burn scar.

Why it matters: Burned slopes above Highway 1 are prone to debris flows and landslides once the winter rains arrive. Knowing where the canopy is gone helps decide which roads, creeks and communities need protection first. Compare with the official fire perimeter, Sentinel-2 burn-severity (dNBR) maps and NASA FIRMS hotspots before treating the outline as the burn scar.

properties.headline: Radar maps a burn scar of about 19 km² in Everglades National Park
properties.subtitle: Drought fires in the sawgrass marshes · Florida
properties.confidence_note: Exploratory thresholds on the drop in L-band cross-polarised radar, not a validated burn map
properties.summary: Comparing NISAR's radar pass on 25 August 2026 with 20 July 2026, before the fire, about 19 km² lost so much cross-polarised signal that it is likely burned, and another 30 km² is possibly burned. Healthy vegetation returns a strong cross-polarised (HV) radar signal from the leaves and stems of sawgrass and other marsh plants; when fire removes them, the signal drops by several decibels.
causes: Fire burning through drought-dried sawgrass and marsh vegetation
Ground fire in exposed peat soils, which can smoulder after the flames pass
Smaller drops can also come from vegetation dying back in the drought, or from water returning to the marsh after rain
properties.why_it_matters: Burned sawgrass usually regrows, but when drought lets fire reach the peat, it burns away soil that took centuries to build, releases stored carbon and changes how water flows through the River of Grass.
properties.next_step: Compare with the park's fire perimeters, Sentinel-2 burn-severity (dNBR) maps and NASA FIRMS hotspots, and check water levels, before treating the outline as the burn scar.
properties.explanation:
NISAR passed over Everglades National Park 6 times between 20 July 2026 and 30 September 2026, all from the same track and look direction so the passes can be compared. Each pass was compared with 20 July 2026, the last pass before the fire started. Healthy vegetation returns a strong cross-polarised (HV) radar signal from the leaves and stems of sawgrass and other marsh plants; when fire removes them, the signal drops by several decibels. Before comparing, the radar brightness was averaged over about 100 m to reduce speckle. Pixels whose HV fell by more than 3 dB are counted as likely burned, and by 2–3 dB as possibly burned.

While the fire was burning, the likely-burned area read 39 km² on 13 August 2026. On 25 August 2026, the first pass after the fire period, it was 19 km², with 30 km² more possibly burned. The last pass, on 30 September 2026, read 411 km², so the area kept growing after the fire period. That can mean the fire was still spreading at its edges, or that scorched vegetation kept drying out and losing its leaves. On the map, the burned patches are filled in two colours, likely and possibly burned; together they cover about 41 km². The story outline is drawn around them.

Fire reports put the fire at about 97 km² (nearly 24,000 acres across four fires in the park, 26 August 2026). The radar's likely-burned area is 19% of that, and 51% with the possibly burned pixels added. A reported fire area is the whole perimeter: it includes unburned islands and ground fire under a canopy that survived, where the radar signal barely changes, so the radar is expected to flag less than the reported area. Source: https://www.wlrn.org/environment/2026-08-26/drought-fire-everglades-peat-national-park.

What this does not say: these are threshold rules on radar brightness, not a verified burn-severity map. Drying vegetation, a change in soil moisture after rain and wind in the vegetation can also lower the signal. In a wetland, standing water returning after rain darkens the radar much as a burn does, so drops in later passes may be water rather than fire. Treat the outline as where to look first, not as the official burn scar.

Why it matters: Burned sawgrass usually regrows, but when drought lets fire reach the peat, it burns away soil that took centuries to build, releases stored carbon and changes how water flows through the River of Grass. Compare with the park's fire perimeters, Sentinel-2 burn-severity (dNBR) maps and NASA FIRMS hotspots, and check water levels, before treating the outline as the burn scar.

properties.headline: Flooding under marsh vegetation is spreading at Lake Manzala
properties.subtitle: Coastal lagoon and reed beds
properties.confidence_note: Exploratory dB thresholds on L-band backscatter, not a validated flood map
properties.summary: Radar measured 2.6% of the analysed area as flooded vegetation on 12 October 2026. That is more than the 2.4% measured on 26 June 2026. Flooded vegetation looks very bright to radar: water and plant stems form a corner that bounces the signal straight back, while the cross-polarised signal stays weak.
causes: Water rising into standing reeds and marsh vegetation
Seasonal flooding of fish farms and marsh margins
Vegetation growing up through shallow standing water
properties.why_it_matters: Lake Manzala is one of Egypt's largest coastal wetlands. How much of it is open water and how much is flooded marsh decides what fishing, farming and wildlife it can support.
properties.next_step: Compare with optical imagery and local water-level records before treating the change as confirmed.
properties.explanation:
NISAR passed over Lake Manzala 9 times between 26 June 2026 and 12 October 2026, all from the same track and look direction so the measurements can be compared. Each pass records two polarisations, HH and HV. Flooded vegetation looks very bright to radar: water and plant stems form a corner that bounces the signal straight back, while the cross-polarised signal stays weak. Pixels brighter than -5 dB in HH whose HH is more than 7 dB above their HV are counted as flooded vegetation.

Across those passes the share of the analysed area classed as flooded vegetation grew from 2.4% to 2.6%, a change of +0.2 percentage points. The lowest reading was 2.3% on 8 July 2026 and the highest 3.4% on 18 September 2026, a trend of about +0.2 percentage points per month. The outline on the map is every part of the area that was flooded vegetation in at least one month, and it covers about 11 km².

What this does not say: these are threshold rules on radar brightness, not a verified flood map. Wind roughening the water surface, wet soil after rain and a different look angle can all move the same numbers. Short, sharp changes between two passes are more likely to be weather or geometry than real change on the ground.

Why it matters: Lake Manzala is one of Egypt's largest coastal wetlands. How much of it is open water and how much is flooded marsh decides what fishing, farming and wildlife it can support. Compare with optical imagery and local water-level records before treating the change as confirmed.
